stocks.note: Numbers as of market close on June 30th.
stocks.news:
Wall Street just closed the books on its best quarter in six years. The S&P 500 climbed 0.79% to 7,499, the NASDAQ jumped 1.52% to 26,213, and the DOW added 0.26% to 52,319 (figures as of the June 30th close). Over the past three months the S&P added roughly $8 trillion in value.

Chips did the heavy lifting. Semiconductor stocks gained about $2 trillion in combined value in the second quarter, their best three months ever, led by names like AMD (+7.68%) and Intel (+6.01%), though the group cooled 7.9% in the final week as investors questioned whether AI spending can keep pace with the buildout. Nike (-1.04%) topped earnings estimates, but a one-time $986 million tariff refund did most of the work after the Supreme Court struck down the original tariff plan.

economy.note: Stock indexes as of the June 30th close; 10-Year, gold, and Brent as of June 30th (Market Briefs); silver is spot as of July 1st (Fortune).
economy.commentary:
Metals eased. Gold slipped 1.23% to $3,989 and silver held near $58.74, up about half a percent, while the 10-year Treasury yield ticked up to 4.46%. Brent crude added 0.47% to $73.29.

The Fourth of July cookout is the priciest on record. Feeding ten now runs about $73.82, a new high, as the U.S. cattle herd sits at a 70-year low and war-related price pressure lingers. Meanwhile President Trump is leaning on gas stations to cut prices to $2.50 a gallon against a national average near $3.86, arguing that crude has fallen but the savings have not reached the pump. For housing, steady energy and a firm 10-year yield keep a floor under mortgage rates for now.

crypto.note: Numbers as of 4:00 PM ET, June 30th.
crypto.commentary:
Crypto edged higher on the day, but the trend is still lower. Bitcoin rose 0.89% to $59,046, Ether added 1.31% to $1,589, and XRP gained 1.03% to $1.05 (figures as of the June 30th close). Even with the daily bounce, Bitcoin is down about 32% year to date.

Strategy (MSTR -6.20%), the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, sold more than $1 billion of its stash this week, and the market followed it lower, with the coin dipping toward $58,000 at one point. On the policy front, crypto firms have already poured $189 million into the 2026 midterms, more than they spent in all of 2024, largely to push the stalled Clarity Act.

real_estate.homebuilder: Mortgage Rates Hold At 6.54% As Home Prices Set Another Record On Near-Flat Growth; Digital Realty Buys Out Blackstone's Data Center Stake For $3.5B; The East Bay Board Eases To 2,805 Active On 177 New And 206 Closed
real_estate.commentary:
The 30-year fixed held at 6.54% and the 15-year stayed at 6.12%. Rates have gone quiet, and so has the resale market, with the lock-in effect still keeping owners in place until the gap to their existing rates narrows.

U.S. home prices set another record high in May, but annual growth was just 0.7%, the ninth straight month under 1%. High rates and thin supply have the market in a standoff: prices are not falling, but they are barely rising either, which leaves buyers and sellers staring at each other with no clear direction.

On the commercial side, Digital Realty (DLR -5.79%) agreed to buy Blackstone's stake in three Virginia data centers for $3.5 billion. The market flinched because the deal leans on $2.3 billion in new stock, diluting existing shareholders, a reminder that even the hottest corner of real estate has a price.

Locally, the East Bay board eased to 2,805 active (down 96 from yesterday), with 177 new listings against 206 closings. Oakland again led the board with 36 new on 744 active; Fremont added 24 new on 339 active.

New-listing flow came in at 177, led by Oakland (36), Fremont (24), and Dublin (19). Closings totaled 206.

For agents: with rates steady and prices flat, the story to tell is stability, not urgency. Lean on the steady supply (2,805 active, 177 new) and price discipline. Well-priced, well-presented homes still sell inside about four weeks, while overpriced listings just sit, so the coaching holds: price to today's market and the sale follows.
